questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Oracle's current cloud-native delivery methodology for Fusion Cloud implementations, organized around phases like Engage, Drive, Design, Configure, Validate, Transition, and Realize, is called Oracle True Cloud Method, abbreviated ________.
questions.explain: Oracle True Cloud Method (TCM) is the cloud-native successor to AIM and OUM, Oracle's on-premise methodologies. It's organized around the phases Engage, Drive, Design, Configure, Validate, Transition, and Realize, guided by the 'adopt, not adapt' principle.

questions.prompt: Brightfield's AP team wants Oracle Fusion configured to exactly replicate their current three-step manual approval workaround, even though Oracle's Modern Best Practice flow already handles equivalent approval routing in two steps. Which response is most consistent with TCM's 'adopt, not adapt' principle?
options: Configure Oracle Fusion to exactly replicate the three-step manual workaround, since matching the legacy process reduces change-management effort
First demonstrate the Modern Best Practice two-step flow against the actual requirement, and only pursue a gap resolution toward a different flow if a genuine business need justifies it
Skip the comparison and automatically build a custom extension that reproduces the exact three-step workaround
Ignore the AP team's current process entirely and configure whatever is fastest to implement, regardless of fit
Have the Solution Architect decide unilaterally, without involving the AP Business Process Owners
Combine Oracle's two-step flow and the legacy three-step workaround into a four-step hybrid process by default
questions.explain: 'Adopt, not adapt' means starting from Oracle's Modern Best Practice reference flow and only deviating where a documented business need genuinely requires it — exactly what fit-gap analysis (Lesson 6) exists to formalize. Replicating a legacy workaround by default, without first testing it against the standard flow, is the opposite of that principle.

questions.prompt: Select every role below that is client-side (Brightfield's own staff), not a partner/consultant-side role, per Lesson 2.
options: Executive Sponsor
Business Process Owner / SME
Solution Architect
Organizational Change Management (OCM) Lead
Technical Consultant
questions.explain: Executive Sponsor, Business Process Owners/SMEs, and the OCM Lead are all client-side roles — Brightfield's own staff who own the business decisions, validate requirements, and manage change. The Solution Architect and Technical Consultant are partner/consultant-side roles who design and build the solution.

questions.prompt: Match each planning document to what it actually captures, per Lesson 3.
right: Breaks the project into workstreams and tasks with owners and target dates
A running log of Risks, Assumptions, Issues, and Dependencies
States the business case, budget, and the Executive Sponsor's authority to make the project happen
The specific modules, legal entities, and countries/currencies actually in scope for this implementation
questions.explain: The Project Charter states the business case, budget, and sponsor authority. The Scope Statement defines exactly which modules, entities, and countries are in scope. The WBS breaks the project into workstreams and tasks with owners. The RAID Log tracks Risks, Assumptions, Issues, and Dependencies throughout the project.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of turning a stakeholder discussion into a usable requirement in the correct order, per Lessons 4 and 5.
items: A facilitator runs a workshop or interview, using a parking lot to capture anything off-topic without derailing the agenda
The discussion is written up as a requirement and sent back to the stakeholders who provided it
Stakeholders sign off that the write-up accurately reflects what was actually discussed
The signed-off requirement is logged in the Business Requirements Document (BRD) with a unique ID
That requirement ID is linked into the Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM), tying it to a future design, configuration, and test script
questions.explain: A workshop or interview surfaces the information first, using a parking lot to stay on track. The write-up goes back to stakeholders for sign-off before anything is treated as final. Only a signed-off requirement gets logged in the BRD with its own ID, which then flows into the RTM linking it forward to design, configuration, and eventually a test script.

questions.prompt: Partway through SIT, the testing lead notices that requirement BR-CM-014 was configured and built, but no test script in the RTM is linked to it. Per Lesson 4, what does this situation actually indicate?
options: Nothing — the RTM only needs to list design and configuration links; test scripts are optional
The requirement was designed and configured but never verified, and this gap should have been caught before testing started
The requirement must have been a process gap rather than a configuration gap
BR-CM-014 should automatically be marked as a fit, since it reached configuration at all
questions.explain: Lesson 4 is explicit: a requirement that can't be traced to a test script by the time testing starts is a red flag — something was designed and configured but never actually proven to work. Ideally, test planning (Lesson 16) catches this gap by checking every RTM row has a linked script, before testing itself begins.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 6, which statement correctly distinguishes a configuration gap from a process gap?
options: A configuration gap closes through a non-default setup choice with no code required; a process gap requires the business process itself to change to align with Oracle's standard functionality

A configuration gap requires the business process itself to change to align with Oracle's standard functionality, which is often considered the harder of the two to close because it needs organizational change management; a process gap, by contrast, closes through a non-default setup choice with no code required
A configuration gap always requires a personalization or an Oracle Integration Cloud extension to close
A process gap is the easiest type to close, since it only requires a non-default setup choice
Both configuration gaps and process gaps always require the Technical Consultant to write code, regardless of classification
A configuration gap can only be identified during User Acceptance Testing, never during the original fit-gap workshop
questions.explain: Lesson 6 defines a configuration gap as something standard functionality can handle, but only with a non-default setup choice rather than code. A process gap, by contrast, is one where Oracle's standard process is capable, but the business itself has to change how it works to align with it — often the harder gap to close because it requires change management, not configuration.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B states the same two definitions as the correct answer, but swaps which gap type each one belongs to. It's actually the process gap that requires the business process itself to change — described in Lesson 6 as often the hardest type to close because it needs organizational change management — while the configuration gap is the one resolved through a non-default setup choice with no code involved.

questions.prompt: Brightfield's gap/solution log lists several proposed fixes. Select every one that correctly matches one of the five solution options from Lesson 7.
options: A configuration change — no cost beyond consultant time already on the project
A personalization — a page-level change within Oracle's supported personalization framework
A permanent code fork of Oracle Fusion's core application, maintained entirely outside Oracle's control
A process workaround — the business adjusts how it works, with no system change
Deferred/backlog — acknowledged, but not solved in this phase
questions.explain: Lesson 7 lists five solution options: configuration, personalization, extension (an OIC process, custom report, or Visual Builder app), process workaround, and deferred/backlog. A permanent fork of Oracle's core application isn't one of them — Oracle Fusion is a multi-tenant SaaS product; customers configure, personalize, and extend it, they don't fork and maintain their own copy of the core application.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the structured document that captures every setup decision — organized by Oracle's own task lists, with sign-off — before anyone touches the live Setup and Maintenance work area, is called a configuration ________.
questions.explain: A configuration workbook captures setup decisions in a reviewable, traceable form, organized to mirror Oracle's task lists, before a consultant keys anything into the live Setup and Maintenance work area.

questions.prompt: Match each Design-phase deliverable to what it actually documents, per Lessons 7, 8, and 10.
right: Narrates the future-state process end to end in business terms, with process flow diagrams
The technical 'how' for each configuration or extension — exactly which object is configured, or the technical build approach
A structured register of every classified gap, its business impact, effort estimate, and proposed solution
Setup object names, attributes, and proposed values organized by Oracle's own task lists, with a sign-off column
questions.explain: The gap/solution log registers every classified gap with its business impact and proposed fix. The configuration workbook captures setup object values by task list, with sign-off. The BPD narrates the future-state process in business terms. The SDD specifies the technical how behind each configuration or extension — what a Technical Consultant actually builds from.

questions.prompt: A project manager suggests finalizing each module's configuration workbook before the enterprise structure (legal entities, business units, ledgers, reference data sets) is approved, to save time. Per Lesson 9, why is this risky?
options: Because every module-level configuration workbook assumes the enterprise structure is already settled, since most setup objects are scoped by a legal entity, business unit, or ledger
Because Oracle Cloud Success Navigator technically prevents any workbook from being created before enterprise structure sign-off
Because enterprise structure decisions are made by the Technical Consultant, not finance leadership, so they have no bearing on module workbooks
Because the configuration workbook format literally cannot include a legal entity or business unit field until the structure is approved
questions.explain: Lesson 9 is explicit that almost every other setup object — bank accounts, payment terms, reconciliation rules, security roles — is scoped by a legal entity, business unit, or ledger. Finalizing a module workbook before that structure is locked risks building on an assumption that later changes, which is exactly why enterprise structure decisions are front-loaded and approved by finance leadership before module workbooks are finalized.

questions.prompt: Put these Chapter 2 deliverables in the order they're actually produced, ending at the phase gate into Configure.
items: Fit-gap analysis classifies each requirement as a fit or a configuration, process, or extension gap
Each gap is logged with a business impact, effort estimate, and proposed solution, then approved or deferred
Enterprise structure decisions (legal entities, business units, ledgers, reference data sets) are locked down and approved
Configuration workbooks capture setup values for every fit and approved configuration gap, organized by task list
The Business Process Design and Solution Design Document are signed off, closing Design and opening Configure
questions.explain: Fit-gap first classifies every requirement. Approved gaps get logged with impact, effort, and a proposed solution. Enterprise structure decisions get locked down early because module-level workbooks depend on them already being settled. Configuration workbooks then capture the actual setup values. Finally, the BPD and SDD synthesize everything into sign-off-ready documents that close Design and open Configure — the phase gate Lesson 3 introduced.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the framework that organizes Oracle Fusion's Setup and Maintenance work area into functional areas, task lists, and tasks is called ________ ________ ________ (FSM).
questions.explain: Functional Setup Manager (FSM) groups related configuration steps into functional areas, which break down into task lists, which contain individual tasks — the same structure a configuration workbook is built to mirror.

questions.prompt: A configuration package scoped to Cash Management is being promoted from Test toward Production. Per Lesson 12, which of these items should the consultant expect to re-point manually in Production rather than assume the package handles automatically?
options: The integration endpoint URL for the bank statement file feed, since it's deliberately environment-specific
The wire transfer auto-match rule's tolerance values, since those never travel with a configuration package
The chart of accounts values, since reference data never travels with a configuration package
The Cash Management task list names themselves, since FSM renames them per environment
questions.explain: Lesson 12 specifically calls out integration endpoint URLs as a value that's deliberately environment-specific and doesn't move automatically with a configuration package — Test points to a test-mode URL, and Production needs its own, manually re-pointed connection. The matching rule's tolerance values and chart of accounts values are ordinary setup data that does travel with the package; task list names are just FSM's fixed organizational structure, not environment-specific data.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Oracle's quarterly update schedule, per Lesson 13.
options: Non-production (Test) environments update on the first Friday of the update month
Production updates two weeks later, on the third Friday of that same month
Every customer's update lands in the exact same calendar week, regardless of cohort
The two-week gap between Test and Production updates exists so a company can test changed features before Production gets them
Once a company goes live, Oracle stops applying quarterly updates to that environment
questions.explain: Test updates on the first Friday of the update month, Production two weeks later on the third Friday — a gap that exists deliberately so new or changed features can be tested in a lower environment first. Customers are grouped into update cohorts (A, B, C) with different calendar months, so not everyone updates the same week. Updates never stop — they apply every quarter for the life of the system, which is exactly why Chapter 4's regression testing lesson exists.

questions.prompt: Match each data migration term to what it actually describes, per Lessons 14 and 15.
right: Closed, fully settled transaction history kept for reporting and audit purposes only
Master data other records depend on, like suppliers and chart of accounts values, loaded first
Still-open items the business needs on day one, like unpaid AP invoices or the GL trial balance
A practice data load, using the same templates and validation steps, run before the real cutover load
questions.explain: Static/reference data is the master data other records depend on, loaded first. Open transactional balances are the still-open items the business needs on day one. Historical/summary data is closed history kept only for reporting. A mock conversion cycle rehearses the real load, with the same templates and validation, before it actually matters.

questions.prompt: Brightfield's first mock load for Cash Management fails for three rows because the legacy bank account numbers include a dash format the FBDI template doesn't accept. Per Lesson 15, what's the correct response?
options: Add a cleansing step that reformats the account numbers before the next mock load, then re-run the mock load and validate again
Skip validation for those three rows and proceed straight to the real cutover load, since the failure is minor
Abandon FBDI entirely and switch to manual entry for all Cash Management bank accounts
Treat the failure as a defect and log it in the testing chapter's defect log instead of fixing the data
questions.explain: This is exactly what Lesson 15 describes happening to Brightfield: a cleansing problem caught in a mock load gets fixed with a cleansing step (reformatting the account numbers), and the next mock load is run and validated again. A mock load failing validation is a good outcome at this stage — it means a cleansing rule needs adjusting, caught weeks before go-live rather than during the real cutover.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a single data migration cycle in the correct order, per Lessons 14 and 15.
items: Cleanse the legacy data — deduplicate, standardize formats, map old codes to the new structure
Build the FBDI file using the cleansed data
Run a mock load of the FBDI file into a non-production environment
Validate the mock load's results against independent legacy source totals
Fix any cleansing or mapping issue the validation surfaces, then repeat the mock load before the real cutover load
questions.explain: Cleansing has to happen before a file is even built, since cleansing against a target structure requires already knowing the mapping. The FBDI file is then built from cleansed data and mock-loaded. Validation reconciles what landed against independent legacy totals, and any issue found gets fixed and re-tested with another mock load — exactly the cycle that caught Brightfield's dash-formatted account numbers before the real cutover load.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 19, which statement correctly distinguishes a defect's severity from its priority?
options: Severity describes a defect's technical impact independent of timing; priority describes how urgently it needs fixing relative to the project's schedule, so a low-severity issue can still be high priority if it's blocking other testing

Priority describes a defect's technical impact independent of timing; severity describes how urgently it needs fixing relative to the project's schedule, so a low-priority issue can still be high severity if it's blocking other testing — the reverse of how the two terms are actually defined
Severity and priority always move together — a high-severity defect is automatically high priority and vice versa
Severity is assigned only by the Testing Lead, while priority is assigned only by the Executive Sponsor
Priority is a technical measure set by Oracle, while severity is a project-management measure set by the implementation team
Severity only applies to defects found in UAT; priority only applies to defects found in SIT
questions.explain: Severity is about technical impact — how badly something breaks the system — independent of when it was found. Priority is about urgency relative to the project's schedule and other open items. That's why a low-severity cosmetic issue can be high priority if it's blocking several other test scripts, and a high-severity issue found early can be lower priority than one found right before cutover.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B states the same relationship as the correct answer but swaps which term is which — it's severity that measures technical impact independent of timing, and priority that measures urgency relative to the project's schedule. Lesson 19 gives the exact example of a high-severity defect found far from go-live getting a lower priority than one found two days before cutover — getting the two terms backwards is the mistake this lesson specifically warns about.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement comparing SIT and UAT, per Lessons 17 and 18.
options: SIT is run by the project team; UAT is run by actual business users
UAT typically includes real business scenarios the business users bring themselves, not just adapted SIT scripts
SIT exists specifically to catch problems that only show up when pieces of the system interact across modules
A formal UAT sign-off certifies the system is completely defect-free
SIT's exit criteria require all critical/high-priority scripts to pass and open defects triaged to an acceptable level
questions.explain: SIT is the project team's own end-to-end, cross-module quality gate before business users get involved; UAT puts actual business users in the driver's seat, running both adapted scripts and their own real scenarios. UAT sign-off certifies the system is ready for the business to run on, not that it's bug-free — minor, lower-severity defects can remain open with an agreed remediation plan, which is exactly why the defect-free claim is false.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: besides scope, levels, environments, and roles, a test plan defines, for each testing level, the ________ — the specific conditions that must be met to start that level and, separately, to formally close it out.
questions.explain: Lesson 16 lists entry and exit criteria as one of the core things a test plan defines for each testing level — for example, SIT's entry criteria require configuration complete and test data loaded, while its exit criteria require scripts passed and defects triaged, before UAT can start.

questions.prompt: Match each testing/defect term to what it actually means, per Lessons 16 and 19.
right: A recurring session reviewing new and unresolved defects to assign severity, priority, and an owner
The technical impact of a defect, independent of timing
The conditions that must be met before a testing level can begin
The conditions that must be met before a testing level can be declared complete
questions.explain: Entry criteria gate the start of a testing level; exit criteria gate its formal close. Severity measures a defect's technical impact, independent of timing. A triage meeting is the recurring session where open defects get a severity, priority, and owner assigned as a group.

questions.prompt: Put these defect life-cycle statuses in the order a defect actually moves through, per Lesson 19.
items: New
Assigned
In Progress
Fixed
Retest
Closed
questions.explain: A defect is logged as New, then Assigned to an accountable developer or consultant, moves to In Progress while actively being worked, becomes Fixed once a fix is applied (usually in a lower environment), enters Retest where the original tester confirms the fix actually works, and only then is marked Closed.

questions.prompt: A quarterly update's readiness notes flag a changed default in a feature Brightfield's Cash Management configuration depends on. Per Lesson 20, what is the correct use of the two-week window between the Test update and the Production update?
options: Review the readiness notes, add the changed scenario to the regression suite, re-run it against the updated Test environment, and decide what to opt into — all before the same update reaches Production
Wait until the update reaches Production, then run the full regression suite there, since Test and Production will behave identically anyway
Run a complete UAT cycle in Test during the two-week window, since regression testing isn't thorough enough for a quarterly update
Ignore the readiness notes until a defect is actually reported in Production, since testing in advance can't catch a changed default
questions.explain: Lesson 20 describes exactly this window being used deliberately: review the update's readiness documentation, re-run the regression suite (including scenarios the update specifically changed) against the updated Test environment, and decide which optional features to opt into — all while Production is still two weeks away from receiving the same update. Waiting for Production or skipping testing in advance defeats the entire purpose of the gap Lesson 13 described.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the moment after which the legacy system stops accepting new transactions related to what's cutting over is called the ________.
questions.explain: The freeze is the defined point after which no new transactions are entered in the legacy system for what's cutting over — without it, final balances migrated into Oracle Fusion would already be stale the moment they load.

questions.prompt: Brightfield's steering committee is deciding whether to proceed to go-live Monday morning. Per Lesson 22, what should that decision actually be grounded in?
options: The cutover validation results — whether the final data load tied out and every rehearsed step completed successfully
A team-wide confidence vote on how the weekend generally felt
Whether the Executive Sponsor personally feels ready, independent of any validation evidence
Whether the cutover rehearsal from several weeks earlier happened to go smoothly
questions.explain: Lesson 22 is explicit that the final go/no-go decision isn't a vote on confidence or morale — it's grounded directly in the cutover's actual validation results: did the final load tie out, and did every rehearsed step complete successfully. The rehearsal (Lesson 21) matters for finding problems ahead of time, but the real go/no-go call is based on this cutover weekend's own evidence, not how a rehearsal went weeks earlier.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement distinguishing hypercare from steady-state production support, per Lessons 23 and 24.
options: Hypercare is staffed by the same implementation team that built the system; steady-state support typically shifts to an internal tiered model
Hypercare responds within hours or same-day; steady-state support generally uses longer, routine response windows
Hypercare has a defined scope, staffing model, and exit criteria agreed before go-live
Hypercare is required to run for exactly thirty calendar days on every implementation, with no exceptions
Hypercare commonly extends through at least one full business cycle, like month-end close, before exit criteria are considered met
questions.explain: Hypercare is staffed by the implementation team itself, with faster, elevated response — unlike steady-state support's internal tiered model and routine response windows. It has defined scope, staffing, and exit criteria set before go-live, not an arbitrary end date — Lesson 23 explicitly warns against ending it on a calendar date alone, and notes it commonly extends through a full business cycle like month-end close. There's no fixed thirty-day rule; duration varies by project complexity.

questions.prompt: Match each support term to what it actually is, per Lesson 24.
right: Oracle itself, reached when an issue looks like a genuine product defect only Oracle can diagnose or fix
A formal support case filed with Oracle through My Oracle Support
An internal help desk or super users, handling how-to questions and simple navigation issues
Internal functional or technical staff who can resolve configuration-level issues
questions.explain: Tier 1 is the internal help desk or super users handling simple how-to questions. Tier 2 is internal functional/technical staff resolving configuration-level issues. Tier 3 is Oracle itself. A Service Request is the formal case filed with Oracle through My Oracle Support once Tiers 1 and 2 have ruled out a configuration or user-error explanation.

questions.prompt: Put these Chapter 5 events in the order they actually happen, from rehearsal through steady-state support.
items: A cutover rehearsal (mock cutover) runs through the entire runbook to validate timing and catch planning problems
The real freeze, final data extract and load, and validation checkpoints run during the actual cutover window
The steering committee makes the final go/no-go decision based on the cutover's validation results
Go-live happens, with the command center triaging real-time issues as business users start transacting
Hypercare provides elevated, implementation-team-staffed support until its exit criteria are met
Steady-state support takes over, organized in Tier 1, Tier 2, and Tier 3, with Oracle Service Requests for genuine product defects
questions.explain: The rehearsal proves out the runbook ahead of time. The real cutover window then runs the freeze, final load, and validation checkpoints for real. The steering committee's go/no-go decision is grounded in that validation evidence. Go-live follows, with the command center handling real-time issues. Hypercare then provides sustained, elevated support until its exit criteria are met, at which point the team hands off to steady-state Tier 1/2/3 support.

questions.prompt: Brightfield's two internal staff who will own Tier 2 support need to be ready to handle configuration-level issues unassisted by the time hypercare ends. Per Lesson 25, what should the knowledge transfer sequence actually look like?
options: The internal staff shadow the implementation's functional consultants first, then reverse-shadow — with the consultants coaching instead of doing — before the implementation team steps back
The implementation team hands over all documentation on the last day of hypercare with no shadowing beforehand, since documentation alone is sufficient
The internal staff reverse-shadow first, coaching the implementation team, and only shadow the consultants afterward
Knowledge transfer only needs to happen if the internal staff will also be delivering end-user training
questions.explain: Lesson 25 describes shadowing (internal staff watching the implementation team work) happening first, followed by reverse shadowing (the implementation team watching and coaching the internal staff) before the partner steps back — exactly the two-week-then-one-week sequence Brightfield used. Reversing that order, or skipping shadowing in favor of documentation alone, doesn't give internal staff the hands-on practice they need to handle issues unassisted.
